content: In countries with a high incidence of tuberculosis (TB), the cumulative prevalence of active TB among household contacts, regardless of their baseline TB infection status, was assessed over a 24-month follow-up period. When compared to the general population, the incidence of TB in household contacts was actively monitored, while cases in the general population were detected passively. This difference in detection methods likely introduced ascertainment bias, potentially overestimating both relative and absolute risks. Additionally, the general population included individuals of all ages, whereas the study population was limited to specific age groups, further complicating comparisons. To estimate the number of TB cases over 24 months, the annual notification rate in the general population was multiplied by a factor of two. The accuracy of the World Health Organization (WHO) symptomatic screening to exclude TB disease in individuals with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) was evaluated. Two studies involving 646 patients used a cross-sectional design to assess test accuracy. The evidence quality was moderate, with no serious concerns about bias, indirectness, or inconsistency, but imprecision was noted. For a pre-test probability of 1%, the test identified 8 true positives per 1,000 patients tested, with 2 false negatives. For a pre-test probability of 5%, the test identified 42 true positives per 1,000 patients tested, with 8 false negatives. For a pre-test probability of 10%, the test identified 85 true positives per 1,000 patients tested, with 15 false negatives. The test also produced a high number of false positives across all pre-test probabilities. In high TB incidence countries, the accuracy of chest X-rays to exclude TB disease in contacts of people with pulmonary TB (without HIV) was assessed. Seven studies involving 25,410 patients used a cross-sectional design. The evidence quality was moderate, with some concerns about study design and indirectness. For a prevalence of 2%, the test identified 1,882 true positives per 100,000 patients, with 118 false negatives. For a prevalence of 5%, the test identified 4,705 true positives per 100,000 patients, with 295 false negatives. The test also produced a significant number of false positives, with 12,936 for a prevalence of 2% and 12,540 for a prevalence of 5%. The predictive value of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) as an alternative to tuberculin skin tests (TSTs) for identifying individuals at the highest risk of progressing from TB infection to active TB disease in high-incidence settings was explored. Longitudinal studies on the predictive value of positive IGRA results are still emerging. The evidence quality was very low, with serious concerns about bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. For example, in one analysis, TST identified 10 more cases per 1,000 individuals tested, while IGRA identified 15 more cases per 1,000 individuals tested, but the confidence intervals were wide, indicating uncertainty. The effectiveness of a 3-month daily rifampicin plus isoniazid regimen (3RH) as a preventive treatment for children and adolescents under 15 years of age was compared to 6or 9-month isoniazid monotherapy (6H or 9H) in high TB incidence countries. The overall quality of evidence was low, with concerns about selection bias, lack of blinding, and imprecision. For example, 3RH was associated with 389 more cases prevented per 1,000 individuals compared to 6H, but the confidence intervals were wide, ranging from 193 to 671 more cases prevented. Adherence rates were higher for 3RH compared to 6H or 9H, but the risk of adverse events was not significantly different. The safety and efficacy of a 4-month daily rifampicin regimen (4R) for preventing TB disease in people of all ages at risk were compared to other recommended regimens, such as 9-month isoniazid (9H). The overall quality of evidence was moderate. In one study, 4R was found to be non-inferior to 9H in preventing active TB, with fewer adverse events and higher treatment completion rates. However, the open-label design of the trials introduced potential performance bias, and some study sites were in low TB incidence settings, limiting generalizability to high-incidence settings. In summary, while shorter regimens like 3RH and 4R show promise in improving adherence and reducing treatment duration, concerns about study design, bias, and imprecision highlight the need for further research to confirm their efficacy and safety in diverse populations and settings.
